digest.intro: Materials remember their origins; so does code, light, and infrastructure under pressure.

items.title: The ad stack as weapons-delivery infrastructure
items.blurb: Citizen Lab confirmed that an Israeli company called Discover-Tech embedded zero-click mercenary spyware inside targeted ads — 45 devices at Al Jazeera were infected without a single tap or click. The attack surface isn't a browser vulnerability or a phishing link; it's the normal programmatic ad-serving pipeline that loads on every website you visit. The implication is structural: the infrastructure that funds the open web is now also a confirmed vector for nation-state-grade surveillance.

items.title: Alberta on the edge: Carney warns of forces trying to 'divide and own' Canada
items.blurb: Canadian PM Mark Carney used unusually sharp language — 'divide and own' — warning that external actors are actively amplifying Alberta's separatism referendum push. A successful vote would be the largest rupture to Canadian political geography since Quebec's 1995 near-miss. Worth watching: this is moving fast enough that the federal government is treating it as an active foreign-influence operation, not just domestic grievance politics.

items.title: Zelensky restarts refinery strikes, calls US moves a betrayal
items.blurb: Ukraine is resuming strikes on Russian oil refineries while Zelensky publicly described recent US posture as a betrayal of Kyiv — a notable hardening of tone toward Washington. Simultaneously, Germany's Merz rejected placing frozen Russian EU assets under US control, insisting those decisions stay European. Two allied capitals are now openly resisting US leverage over war resources in the same week.

sections.heading: Materials, forms, and the things we make

items.title: What on Earth Is Dekton?
items.blurb: Charles Mann traces how a $150/sq ft engineered surface called Dekton — invented by Spanish company Cosentino in 2013 and now ubiquitous in high-end kitchens and architecture — is, at its core, just porcelain made under pressures and temperatures that would have been industrially impossible thirty years ago. The essay becomes a deep history of porcelain itself as one of humanity's longest-running high-tech obsessions, moving between Song dynasty kilns and modern sintering chambers without losing the thread. It's the kind of piece where you start wondering about your countertop and end up understanding how materials encode civilization.

items.title: Venus' flower basket, solved after 185 years
items.blurb: The glass sponge Euplectella aspergillum has lived at 500m depth for millennia with a skeleton that simultaneously manages structural load and fluid flow — two properties that normally trade off against each other in engineering. Berkeley and Harvard researchers built an automated simulation framework that finally cracked how it does both at once, then used that insight to design metamaterials that do the same. The result is the first dual-optimized mechano-fluidic material, with direct applications to aerostructures and biostructures.

items.title: This Resin 3D Printer Changed My Mind
items.blurb: CNC Kitchen is the only 3D printing channel that earns the phrase 'changed my mind' — everything he says is backed by tensile testing and mechanical data rather than vibes. When he recants on a whole printer category, it's worth 20 minutes to find out why.

items.title: Neural networks are already clean
items.blurb: Goodfire's researchers spent months staring at individual neurons in image and language models and came back with a surprising finding: the canonical evidence for 'polysemanticity' — the idea that neurons are hopelessly entangled, doing multiple unrelated jobs — was mostly misread. What looked like arbitrary packing turns out to be a legible pattern they call 'recursive generalization,' which is far less alarming and far more interpretable. The practical upshot: you may be able to study what a network is doing directly, without first untangling it through sparse autoencoders or feature extraction.

items.title: Meta's 816B open-weights agent model runs on two Mac Studios
items.blurb: Muse Spark Open drops today: 816B total parameters, 42B active (MoE), 1M-token context, open weights, optimized for Apple M5 Ultra via MLX — meaning two Mac Studios can run a frontier-class agentic model locally. The benchmark story matters less than the structural shift: open weights for a model genuinely capable of long-horizon agentic tasks changes who can build autonomous systems without API dependency. This is the kind of release that quietly moves the floor for what independent builders can do.

items.title: Folders: a programming language made entirely of directory structure
items.blurb: Daniel Temkin — a legitimate artist working the code-as-expression seam — built a programming language where the entire program is encoded in folder hierarchy. No files, no text, no syntax: the structure of nested directories is the code. It's concept art that actually executes, and a clean provocation about what 'writing' a program even means when you strip away every surface that looks like language.

facts.fact: Citizen Lab confirmed 45 devices at Al Jazeera were infected with mercenary spyware delivered through normal targeted ads — requiring zero clicks from the targets.
Dekton, now common in high-end architecture, costs roughly five times as much per square foot as tempered glass and was impossible to manufacture industrially before the 1990s.

The glass sponge Euplectella aspergillum has lived at depths below 500 meters, often for millennia, with a skeleton that simultaneously optimizes for structural load and fluid flow — a dual-property combination engineers had never achieved until now.
Meta's Muse Spark Open has 816 billion total parameters but only 42 billion active at inference (mixture-of-experts), and is the first frontier-class model designed to run on consumer Apple Silicon.

The canonical example of an 'impossible to interpret' polysemantic neuron — one that responded to both cat faces and car fronts — may have been misread; Goodfire researchers argue it reflects a learnable pattern called recursive generalization, not arbitrary entanglement.

art_picks.title: Wavelength
art_picks.creator: Michael Snow
art_picks.why: A 45-minute single zoom across a Manhattan loft — structural cinema as a meditation on time, space, and perception. It doesn't tell a story so much as reveal one system (the room, the shot, the viewer's attention) collapsing into another. Exactly the kind of obsessive, unreasonably narrow project that opens a door.

art_picks.title: Black Origami
art_picks.creator: Jlin
art_picks.why: Footwork evolved into something closer to a generative rendering algorithm — polyrhythmic structures so dense they feel architectural, like watching a 3D object rotate in impossible dimensions. Pure expressive system with no wasted surface.

art_picks.title: Line Describing a Cone (and solid light works)
art_picks.creator: Anthony McCall
art_picks.why: Projected light turned into inhabitable 3D sculpture — you walk inside a volumetric cone of haze and beam and your body becomes part of the drawing. The edge where cinema, sculpture, and real-time perception collapse into one thing; the physical/digital boundary at its most elemental.

events.name: Anthony McCall: Solid Light, 1973, 2020, 2026
events.venue: Sean Kelly Gallery, 475 Tenth Avenue, Chelsea
events.why: Three milestone solid-light works spanning fifty years — including the world premiere of Swarm (2026) and the gallery's first showing of the iconic Line Describing a Cone — haze-filled rooms where projected light becomes physical, walkable sculpture.

events.name: Lee Bul: The Anatomy of Every Setting Sun
events.why: Monumental sculptures that look like fragments of shattered utopian architecture — Lee Bul is working exactly at the seam of technology, futurism, and the body; closes Oct 24 so go now.

events.name: Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous
events.venue: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, 1000 Fifth Avenue
events.why: 120+ works placing both artists in genuine dialogue rather than the usual Pollock-overshadows-Krasner frame — a rare chance to see two intertwined systems of mark-making examined on equal terms.

events.name: Contemporaneous / Recap Percussion / Mantra Percussion: Seeing in the Dark
events.why: Three percussion-forward new music ensembles sharing a stage at Roulette — the room where avant-garde NYC still happens without corporate scaffolding; expect structured chaos with genuine compositional ambition.

events.name: Unsound New York
events.venue: Lincoln Center (multiple venues incl. Alice Tully Hall & Atrium)
events.why: The NYC edition of Krakow's genre-dissolving experimental festival — this year featuring emo-ambient composer claire rousay with Polish minimalist Martyna Basta, and the hallucinatory vocal/sound duo FUJIIIIIIIIIIITA and Ka Baird; the kind of thing that rewires what music can feel like.
